(1960) | | _**The Shape of Jazz to Come**_ is the third studio album by the American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") musician [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"). Released on [Atlantic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Records "Atlantic Records") in November 1959, it was his debut on the label and his first album featuring the quartet of himself, trumpeter [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), bassist [Charlie Haden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Haden "Charlie Haden"), and drummer [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-3) The recording session for the album took place on May 22, 1959, at [Radio Recorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Recorders "Radio Recorders") in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Kaplan,_Fred_M._2009-4) Although Coleman initially wished for the album to be titled _Focus on Sanity_ after its fourth track, producer [Nesuhi Ertegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesuhi_Ertegun "Nesuhi Ertegun") suggested the final title, feeling that it would give consumers "an idea about the uniqueness of the LP."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Kaplan,_Fred_M._2009-4) In 2012, the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") added _The Shape of Jazz to Come_ to the [National Recording Registry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Recording_Registry "National Recording Registry").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-5) The album was included in all three editions of the _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ list of [the 500 greatest albums of all time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-genius.com-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-:0-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-:1-8) [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") called it one of the 20 essential [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") albums.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Free_Jazz:_A_Subjective_History-9) The album was inducted into [the Grammy Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Hall_of_Fame_Award "Grammy Hall of Fame Award") in 2015.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-GRAMMY_Hall_Of_Fame-10) ## Background From 1948 to 1958, Coleman moved between [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"), his hometown of [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"), and [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), working various jobs and developing his own unique sound that was often met with hostility.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-pbs-grove-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-12) His approach initially made it difficult for him to make ends meet by playing music.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shape_of_Jazz_to_Come#cite_note-Johnson,_Martin_2009-13) While employed as an elevator operator in Los Angeles, he studied [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and harmony and developed an idiosyncratic take on [country blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_blues "Country blues") and [folk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music "Folk music") (1965) | | _**Spiritual Unity**_ is a 1965 [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_album "Studio album") by the American [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") saxophonist [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"). It was recorded on July 10, 1964, with bassist [Gary Peacock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Peacock "Gary Peacock") and drummer [Sunny Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Murray "Sunny Murray"). It was the first album recorded for [Bernard Stollman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Stollman "Bernard Stollman")'s [ESP-Disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESP-Disk "ESP-Disk") label, and it brought the "shockingly different" Ayler to international attention.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-wilmer139-2) It also established ESP-Disk as "a major source for [avant-garde jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_jazz "Avant-garde jazz")".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-DeVeaux-3) ## Background In late December 1963, Bernard Stollman, who had been toying with the idea of starting a record label, went, at the insistence of a friend, to hear Ayler at the Baby Grand Café on 125th Street in Harlem.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-4) Ayler had moved to New York City earlier in the year, and had recently been playing with a variety of musicians, including [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), with whom Ayler made an informal recording earlier that month,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-5) and [Cecil Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Taylor "Cecil Taylor"), with whom he would perform on New Years Eve on a concert at Philharmonic Hall, [Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Center "Lincoln Center") that would also feature the [John Coltrane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Coltrane "John Coltrane") quintet and [Art Blakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Blakey "Art Blakey") and [the Jazz Messengers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jazz_Messengers "The Jazz Messengers").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-6) According to Stollman, upon arriving at the Baby Grand Cafe, > Elmo Hope was at the piano, with his trio, on an elevated stage. I sat and listened to them. Several minutes later, a small man in a gray leather suit, holding a large saxophone, brushed by me and jumped up on the stage. He had a black beard, with a little patch of white in it. He was not introduced and, ignoring the trio, he began to blow his horn. The other musicians stopped and looked at him. No words were exchanged. Elmo Hope quietly closed his piano, the bass player parked his bass, the drummer put his sticks down, and they all sat back to listen. He was playing solo, and he kept right on playing for twenty to thirty minutes, just a burst of music. It seemed like a second; it was no time at all! Then he stopped and jumped down from the platform, covered with sweat.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) Stollman then approached Ayler, told him he was starting a record label, and asked him to be his first artist, offering a $500 advance.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-8) Ayler agreed, and stated that he would contact Stollman after fulfulling a commitment to record material at Atlantic Studios.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-weiss21-7) In early 1964, Ayler briefly joined a quartet led by [Paul Bley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Bley "Paul Bley").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-schwartz-9) This occasion introduced Ayler to bassist Gary Peacock, who had been playing with Bley for several years, and who had also recently recorded with [Bill Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Evans "Bill Evans"). Bley's group also included drummer Sunny Murray, with whom Ayler had played in Cecil Taylor's group.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-schwartz-9) The Bley quartet did not record, and made only one public appearance at the Take 3 coffeehouse in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-schwartz-9) By late spring, Ayler, Peacock, and Murray had formed a trio after Peacock left [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' group, where he was substituting for [Ron Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Carter "Ron Carter").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Unity#cite_note-10) On June 14, the trio played at the Cellar Café in New York and recorded the material that would be released on the album _[Prophecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophecy_(Albert_Ayler_album) "Prophecy (Albert Ayler album)")_, which features some of the pieces that would be recorded for _Spiritual Unity_ less than a month later. ## Recording and release [... middle omitted — see footer ...] _[Swing Low Sweet Spiritual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_Low_Sweet_Spiritual "Swing Low Sweet Spiritual")_ (1964)

(1970) | | _**Emergency!**_ is the debut [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") by the American [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") group [the Tony Williams Lifetime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tony_Williams_Lifetime "The Tony Williams Lifetime") featuring Williams with guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)") and organist [Larry Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Young_(musician) "Larry Young (musician)"). It was recorded and released in 1969 and was one of the first significant [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") recordings.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-2) The album is commonly regarded as an influential album in the [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music"), and [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusion_(music) "Fusion (music)") genres.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-3) ## Composition \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emergency!_(album)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Composition")\] According to jazz scholar Christopher Meeder, the Lifetime eschewed the funk influence of [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis")' early fusion music with a mixture of heavy rock drumming and the "light, rapid [swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_(jazz_performance_style) "Swing (jazz performance style)")" that was Williams' signature. " _Emergency!_ synthesized the best elements of [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), [modal jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_jazz "Modal jazz"), and [British rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_rock "British rock")", Meeder wrote, "and added a rhythmic complexity in tracks like 'Via the Spectrum Road,' a blues of sorts in the [unusual time signature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_signature#Complex_time_signatures "Time signature") of 11/8."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Meeder-4) In [Paul Hegarty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hegarty_(musician) "Paul Hegarty (musician)")'s opinion, the music was more oriented with [progressive music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_music "Progressive music")'s rock side rather than its jazz, fusing psychedelic elements while featuring "reprises, crescendos, an oscillation between the simpler time signatures of rock and the more progressive metres of jazz". He cited "Via the Spectrum Road" as an example of how Williams' singing approached the "non-rock, non-jazz softness" of progressive rock pioneer [Robert Wyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Wyatt "Robert Wyatt").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-5) "Via the Spectrum Road" was viewed by [Stuart Nicholson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Nicholson_(jazz_historian) "Stuart Nicholson (jazz historian)") as one of the album's most blatant explorations of rock rhythms. "Spectrum", on the other hand, utilized rhythms from [post-bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-bop "Post-bop"). Composed by McLaughlin, it was first recorded for his 1969 _[Extrapolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrapolation_(album) "Extrapolation (album)")_ debut and was regarded by Nicholson as an extension of that album's "free-flowing approach ... but reinforced by the volume and energy associated with rock".[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-6) A mistake during _Emergency_'s production led Meeder to believe it helped lend a "raw power" to the music: "A cynical engineer used to recording mainstream jazz recorded the band carelessly, allowing the tape to distort, unintentionally adding satisfyingly raw edges to the album."[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!_(album)#cite_note-Meeder-4) ## Release and reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Emergency!_(album)&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Release and reception")\] | Review scores | | --- | | Source | Rating | [... middle omitted — see footer ...] [Categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Category "Help:Category"): - 1976 North American edition | | | | | _**Agharta**_ is a 1975 live [double album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_album "Double album") by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") trumpeter, composer, and bandleader [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). By the time he recorded the album, Davis was 48 years old and had alienated many in the jazz community while attracting younger [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") audiences with his radical electric [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion") music. After experimenting with different line-ups, he established a stable live band in 1973 and toured constantly for the next two years, despite physical pain from worsening health and emotional instability brought on by substance abuse. During a three-week tour of Japan in 1975, the trumpeter performed two concerts at the [Festival Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_Hall,_Osaka "Festival Hall, Osaka") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka") on February 1; the afternoon show produced _Agharta_, and the evening show was released as _[Pangaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea_(album) "Pangaea (album)")_ the following year. Davis led a [septet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Septet "Septet") at the concert; he, saxophonist [Sonny Fortune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonny_Fortune "Sonny Fortune"), and guitarist [Pete Cosey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Cosey "Pete Cosey") were given space to improvise against a dense backdrop of [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff_(music) "Riff (music)"), electronic effects, [cross-beats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-beat "Cross-beat"), and [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") [grooves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groove_(music) "Groove (music)") from the [rhythm section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_section "Rhythm section") – drummer [Al Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Foster "Al Foster"), bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), guitarist [Reggie Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggie_Lucas "Reggie Lucas"), and percussionist [James Mtume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Mtume "James Mtume"). Davis controlled their rhythmic and musical direction with hand and head gestures, [phrases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrase_(music) "Phrase (music)") played on his [wah-wah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah-wah_pedal "Wah-wah pedal") processed trumpet, and [drones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_(music) "Drone (music)") from an accompanying [electronic organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_organ "Electronic organ"). The evolving nature of the performance led to the widespread misunderstanding that it had no compositional basis, while its dark, angry, and somber musical qualities were seen as a reflection of the bandleader's emotional and spiritual state at the time. _Agharta_ was first released in Japan by [CBS/Sony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music_Entertainment_Japan "Sony Music Entertainment Japan") in August 1975 just before Davis temporarily retired due to increasingly poor health and exhaustion. At the record label's suggestion, it was titled after [the legendary subterranean city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agharta "Agharta"). Davis enlisted Japanese artist [Tadanori Yokoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadanori_Yokoo "Tadanori Yokoo") to design its artwork, which depicted the cityscape of an advanced civilization with elements inspired by [Eastern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_world "Eastern world") subterranean myths, [Afrofuturism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrofuturism "Afrofuturism"), and [ufology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ufology "Ufology"). An alternate cover was produced for its 1976 release in North America by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). (1973) | | _**On the Corner**_ is a studio album by the American jazz trumpeter, bandleader, and composer [Miles Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_Davis "Miles Davis"). It was recorded in June and July 1972 and released on October 11 of that year by [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records"). The album continued Davis' exploration of [jazz fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_fusion "Jazz fusion"), and explicitly drew on the [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk") of [Sly Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sly_Stone "Sly Stone") and [James Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Brown "James Brown"), the [experimental music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_music "Experimental music") of [Karlheinz Stockhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karlheinz_Stockhausen "Karlheinz Stockhausen"), the [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") of [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), and the work of collaborator [Paul Buckmaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Buckmaster "Paul Buckmaster").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-1) Recording sessions for the album featured a changing lineup of musicians including bassist [Michael Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Henderson "Michael Henderson"), guitarist [John McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McLaughlin_(musician) "John McLaughlin (musician)"), and keyboardists [Chick Corea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chick_Corea "Chick Corea") and [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock"), with Davis playing his trumpet through a [wah-wah pedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wah-wah_pedal "Wah-wah pedal").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Christgau-2) Davis and producer [Teo Macero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teo_Macero "Teo Macero") then [spliced and edited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reel-to-reel_audio_tape_recording#As_a_musical_instrument "Reel-to-reel audio tape recording") various takes into compositions. The album's packaging did not credit any musicians, in an attempt to make the instruments less discernible to critics. Its artwork features [Corky McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corky_McCoy "Corky McCoy")'s cartoon designs of urban [African-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans") characters. _On the Corner_ was in part an effort by Davis to reach a younger African-American audience who had largely left jazz for funk and rock music; instead, due to Columbia's lack of [target marketing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_market "Target market"), it was one of Davis' worst-selling albums, and was scorned by jazz critics and many of Davis' contemporaries at the time of its release.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Chinen-4) It would be Davis's last studio album of the 1970s conceived as a complete work; subsequently, he recorded haphazardly and focused on live performance before temporarily retiring in 1975.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-5) Critical and popular reception of _On the Corner_ has improved dramatically with the passage of time.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Corner#cite_note-Reynolds-6) Many outside the jazz community have since called it an innovative musical statement anticipating subsequent developments in styles including funk, jazz, [post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk"), [electronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronica "Electronica"), and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop"). In 2007, _On the Corner_ was reissued as part of the six-disc box set _[The Complete On the Corner Sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Complete_On_the_Corner_Sessions "The Complete On the Corner Sessions")_. ## Background [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Miles_Davis-140916-0016-103WP_(cropped).jpg) Davis performing in Germany, 1971 [... middle omitted — see footer ...] "Super Nova (Wayne Shorter album)")_

It is oriented towards straight [bebop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebop "Bebop"), and slightly less adventurous than the majority of his later recordings.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-Simosko44-4) The album was recorded at [Van Gelder Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Gelder_Studio "Van Gelder Studio") in New Jersey and features Dolphy in a quintet with trumpeter [Freddie Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freddie_Hubbard "Freddie Hubbard"), pianist [Jaki Byard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaki_Byard "Jaki Byard"), bassist [George Tucker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Tucker_(musician) "George Tucker (musician)") and drummer [Roy Haynes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Haynes "Roy Haynes"). Hubbard had shared living space with Dolphy when they both first arrived in New York City.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-5) The cover artwork was by Dolphy's friend [Richard "Prophet" Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Slater_Jennings "Richard Slater Jennings").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-6) Of the three Dolphy originals on the album, "G.W." is dedicated to the [Californian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") bandleader [Gerald Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Wilson "Gerald Wilson"),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-Simosko44-4) "Les" is named after the [trombonist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trombone "Trombone") Lester Robertson,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-payne-7) and "245" was the number of Dolphy's house on Carlton Avenue, in Brooklyn's [Fort Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Greene,_Brooklyn "Fort Greene, Brooklyn") neighborhood.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)#cite_note-8) ## Reception \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Reception")\] [... middle omitted — see footer ...] Retrieved from " [https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Outward\_Bound\_(Eric\_Dolphy\_album)&oldid=1209926953](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Outward_Bound_(Eric_Dolphy_album)&oldid=1209926953)" [Categories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Category "Help:Category"): - ( [Dubois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Dubois "Eugène Dubois"), 1893) | _**Homo erectus**_ ([/ˌhoʊmoʊəˈrɛktəs/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")lit.'[upright](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/erectus "wikt:erectus") man') is an [extinct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extinction "Extinction") [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species "Species") of [archaic human](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo "Homo") from the [Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleistocene "Pleistocene"), spanning nearly 2 million years. It is the first human species to evolve a humanlike [body plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_plan "Body plan") and [gait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_gait "Human gait"), to [leave Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_expansions_of_hominins_out_of_Africa "Early expansions of hominins out of Africa") and colonize Asia and Europe, and to [wield fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans "Control of fire by early humans"). Some populations of _H. erectus_ were ancestors of later human species, including _[H. heidelbergensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_heidelbergensis "Homo heidelbergensis")_—the [last common ancestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_common_ancestor "Last common ancestor") of [modern humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human"), [Neanderthals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal"), and [Denisovans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan "Denisovan"). As such a widely distributed species both geographically and temporally, _H. erectus_ anatomy varies considerably. Subspecies are sometimes recognized: _[H. e. erectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_Man "Java Man")_, _[H. e. pekinensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking_Man "Peking Man")_, _[H. e. soloensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_Man "Solo Man")_, _[H. e. ergaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_ergaster "Homo ergaster")_, _[H. e. georgicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmanisi_hominins "Dmanisi hominins")_, and _[H. e. tautavelensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tautavel_Man "Tautavel Man")_. # European free jazz European free jazz Music genre | | | | --- | --- | | ![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f2/Edit-clear.svg/120px-Edit-clear.svg.png) | This article's style of writing **may not reflect the [encyclopedic tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles") used on Wikipedia**. See Wikipedia's [guide to writing better articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing_better_articles#Tone "Wikipedia:Writing better articles") for suggestions._(May 2026)__([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance_template_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_ | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/39/Bailey1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bailey1.jpg) [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)") **European free jazz** is a part of the global [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz") scene with its own development and characteristics. It is hard to establish who are the founders of European free jazz because of the different developments in different European countries. One can, however, make an argument that European free jazz took its development from American [free jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_jazz "Free jazz"), where musicians such as [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman") revolutionised the way of playing. As the British drummer [Eddie Prévost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Pr%C3%A9vost "Eddie Prévost"), of long-standing improvising ensemble AMM, has put it, 'the music of Ornette Coleman and Albert Ayler gave us _permission to disobey_.'[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-1) Yet at much the same time, there were significant European innovations: for example, the same year as Coleman's [_Free Jazz_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Jazz:_A_Collective_Improvisation "Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation") album was released (1961), in the UK the Jamaican alto saxophonist [Joe Harriott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Harriott "Joe Harriott") released the first of his experimental albums, _[Free Form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Form_(Joe_Harriott_album) "Free Form (Joe Harriott album)")._ It was recorded in late 1960, the month before Coleman's.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-2) ## American origin Free jazz got its name from the album _Free Jazz_ (Atlantic, 1961) by Ornette Coleman to describe American avant-garde jazz of the 1960s.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Besides "avant-garde", it was called "the New Wave", "the New Thing", "action jazz", and in Europe "improvised music".[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Germans played a form of free jazz that had something in common with the [aleatoric music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleatoric_music "Aleatoric music") of [Bernd Alois Zimmermann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernd_Alois_Zimmermann "Bernd Alois Zimmermann") and was performed by [Derek Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Bailey_(guitarist) "Derek Bailey (guitarist)"), [Joachim Kuhn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Kuhn "Joachim Kuhn"), [Albert Mangelsdorff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mangelsdorff "Albert Mangelsdorff"), [Manfred Schoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_Schoof "Manfred Schoof"), [John Surman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surman "John Surman"), and [Alexander von Schlippenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_von_Schlippenbach "Alexander von Schlippenbach").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) Free jazz was unpopular and didn't sell well.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-New_Grove1-3) It was viewed as a musical, political, and social backlash to the structure of jazz and of American society at the time. "For some performers the style was loosely linked to the [Black Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Power "Black Power") movement in the USA, partly because of the radical political outlook of some of its practitioners and advocates (e.g., [Archie Shepp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Shepp "Archie Shepp") and [LeRoi Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeRoi_Jones "LeRoi Jones") – later known as Amiri Baraka) and partly owing to the explosive, expressionistic nature of the music itself".[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-4) Due to the lack of commercial success of the free jazz music as well as the racial issues, like the [Civil Rights Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement"), many American free jazz musicians began touring the European continent, playing and spreading their new avant-garde style throughout Europe.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-autogenerated1-5) Jazz musicians like Ornette Coleman, [Albert Ayler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Ayler "Albert Ayler"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), [Bud Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Powell "Bud Powell"), [Don Byas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Byas "Don Byas") traveled and performed throughout Europe.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-6) In contrast to the lack of commercial success in America, many American free jazz musicians experienced both commercial success and acceptance in Europe, leading to tours of Europe and extended residencies.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-7) "A number of jazz musicians migrated to other parts of the world, where they received an opposite response, being considered the ultimate expression of high culture. Thus, many of them remained in exile, and they enjoyed unparalleled success in France, Germany, Japan, Scandinavia, and the Netherlands after the world wars".[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_free_jazz#cite_note-8) [... middle omitted — see footer ...] | Related | - [Acid jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_jazz "Acid jazz")

Early life \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Early life")\] Tapscott was born in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"), and moved to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), at the age of nine.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) By this time he had begun to study piano and trombone.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) He played with [Frank Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Morgan_(musician) "Frank Morgan (musician)"), [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(trumpeter) "Don Cherry (trumpeter)"), Bobby Bradford, and [Billy Higgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Higgins "Billy Higgins") as a teenager. ## Soon after, though, he quit playing trombone and focused on piano.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) In 1961, Tapscott formed the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra,[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-5) with the aim of preserving, developing and performing African-American music. Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Sinclair "Guido Sinclair") all performed in Tapscott's Arkestra at one time or another.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-ucla-bio-2) Tapscott and his work are the subjects of the [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles") Horace Tapscott Jazz Collection.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-oac-6) Enthusiasts of his music formed two labels in the 1970s and 1980s, Interplay and Nimbus, for which he recorded.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-Grove-4) From [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic"): "His pianistic technique was hard and percussive, likened by some to that of [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk") and [Herbie Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Nichols "Herbie Nichols") and every bit as distinctive. In contexts ranging from freely improvised duos to highly arranged big bands, Tapscott exhibited a solo and compositional voice that was his own." ## Death and legacy \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Horace_Tapscott&action=edit§ion=3 "Edit section: Death and legacy")\] Having been suffering from brain cancer, Tapscott died aged 64 on February 27, 1999, the day before a planned tribute concert in his honor took place at Los Angeles' [Leimert Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leimert_Park,_Los_Angeles "Leimert Park, Los Angeles").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-7) An engraving in the sidewalk along Degnan Boulevard in the Leimert Park neighborhood reads: "Horace Tapscott, the local pianist and organizer whose ensemble, the Pan Afrikan Peoples Arkestra, gave many musicians their first gigs and helped heal a community impacted by racism."[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-8) His personal archive of manuscripts, arrangements and recordings was donated to [UCLA Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA_Library "UCLA Library") in 2003 by his wife, Cecilia Tapscott.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tapscott#cite_note-9) ## Discography [... middle omitted — see footer ...] - BAG is known for the convergence of free jazz and experimental theater.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-washu-thesource-bag-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-looker-bag-book-2) ## Members Members included saxophonists [Julius Hemphill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Hemphill "Julius Hemphill"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) [Oliver Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lake "Oliver Lake"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) [Lester Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bowie "Lester Bowie"), [J. D. Parran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._D._Parran "J. D. Parran"), [Hamiet Bluiett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamiet_Bluiett "Hamiet Bluiett"), and [Luther Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luther_Thomas "Luther Thomas"); trumpeters [Baikida Carroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikida_Carroll "Baikida Carroll")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) and [Floyd LeFlore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floyd_LeFlore "Floyd LeFlore"); trombonist [Joseph Bowie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Bowie "Joseph Bowie");[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) drummers [Bensid Thigpen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bensid_Thigpen?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bensid Thigpen") and [Charles "Bobo" Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_%22Bobo%22_Shaw "Charles \"Bobo\" Shaw");[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) bassist Bobby Reed, [Arzinia Richardson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arzinia_Richardson?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arzinia Richardson"); stage directors [Malinke Robert Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malinke_Robert_Elliott?action=edit&redlink=1 "Malinke Robert Elliott"), [Vincent Terrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Terrell?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vincent Terrell"), and [Muthal Naidoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muthal_Naidoo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Muthal Naidoo"); actors [LeRoi S. Shelton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeRoi_S._Shelton?action=edit&redlink=1 "LeRoi S. Shelton"); poets [Ajule (Bruce) Rutlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajule_(Bruce)_Rutlin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ajule (Bruce) Rutlin")[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Artists_Group#cite_note-LarkinJazz-3) and [Shirley LeFlore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_LeFlore "Shirley LeFlore"); dancers [Georgia Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Collins?action=edit&redlink=1 "Georgia Collins") and [Luisah Teish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luisah_Teish "Luisah Teish"); and painters [Emilio Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilio_Cruz_(artist) "Emilio Cruz (artist)") and [Oliver Lee Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lee_Jackson "Oliver Lee Jackson"). (1959) | | _**Tomorrow Is the Question!**_, subtitled _The New Music of Ornette Coleman!_, is the second album by American [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") musician [Ornette Coleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornette_Coleman "Ornette Coleman"), originally released in 1959 by [Contemporary Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_Records "Contemporary Records"). As well as regular sideman [Don Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Cherry_(jazz) "Don Cherry (jazz)") on trumpet, the album features bassists [Percy Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Heath "Percy Heath") and [Red Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Mitchell "Red Mitchell"), and drummer [Shelly Manne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shelly_Manne "Shelly Manne"). ## Reception | Review scores | | --- | | Source | Rating | | [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") | ![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![Star](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/40px-Star_full.svg.png)![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Star_empty.svg/40px-Star_empty.svg.png)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomorrow_Is_the_Question!#cite_note-1) | | [Yahoo! The album features performances by Taylor with [Buell Neidlinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buell_Neidlinger "Buell Neidlinger"), [Denis Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Charles "Denis Charles") and [Steve Lacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lacy_(saxophonist) "Steve Lacy (saxophonist)"). ## Music \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jazz_Advance&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Music")\] The album contains three Taylor originals, three [standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_standard "Jazz standard"), and one standard-to-be, [Thelonious Monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thelonious_Monk "Thelonious Monk")'s " [Bemsha Swing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bemsha_Swing "Bemsha Swing")," first recorded only four years before Taylor's version. This track is played "cryptically and succinctly, the lines breaking up into jagged fragments and jutting chords." "Charge 'Em Blues" is in **4** **4** time. The chords and light treble playing towards the beginning of "Azure" are similar to the sound of [Abdullah Ibrahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdullah_Ibrahim "Abdullah Ibrahim"), but then "the cross-rhythmic improvised piano patterns clattering chords typical of later Taylor emerge."[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz_Advance#cite_note-1) ## Reception \[
